problems.label: Opioid use with withdrawal and overdose risk

definitions.text: Uses opioids more than planned or prescribed, and has tried to stop without success.
Feels sick, achy and has strong cravings when not using.
Is at risk of overdose, for example from using alone, fentanyl exposure, mixing with sedatives or a recent break in use.

longTermGoals.text: The client is alive and safer, on effective treatment if they choose it, and rebuilding health, relationships and daily life.

shortTermObjectives.text: By the next session, have naloxone at home and show how to use it to one other person.
Within 1 week, attend an appointment with a prescriber or opioid treatment program to discuss medication.
Stay on medication treatment, if chosen, and attend at least 80% of scheduled appointments for 3 months.
By session 3, describe personal reasons for change and one goal for the next month.
Use a coping skill for at least 3 cravings a week and record the outcome.
By session 2, complete a safety plan that includes overdose risk and suicidal thoughts.

problems.label: Building daily life, relationships and supports that make change in opioid use last

definitions.text: Most free time, friends or routines are linked to opioid use, and other rewarding activities have dropped away.
Has few people who support the change, or relationships at home are strained by use.

longTermGoals.text: The client has rewarding activities, relationships and supports that fit the goal they chose.

shortTermObjectives.text: With a clinician trained in the community reinforcement approach, by week 6 plan at least 2 rewarding activities a week without opioid (for example work, social or leisure) and a trial period without use that the client agrees to.

By week 4, explore mutual-help options that fit the client (for example NA, SMART Recovery, or faith-based or culturally specific groups) and, if interested, attend at least 1 meeting and talk it over at the next session.
If the client has a partner who supports the change and there is no abuse or coercive control, discuss by week 4 behavioral couples therapy, and refer if it fits.
If trauma symptoms and opioid use feed each other, discuss by week 6 integrated treatment for both, alongside medication treatment.
If chronic pain is part of the picture, discuss with the prescriber, with consent, a pain plan that includes psychological approaches such as a mindfulness-based group program.

collaborativeNote: Write goals and objectives with the client in their own words. Timelines and targets are examples to adapt; the client decides what matters, and the clinician checks safety and fit. Every item in this plan records substance use: the export carries the 42 CFR Part 2 notice.
